name: General trivia (hard)
description: 50 hard questions about a broad mix of everyday knowledge that fits none of the other categories. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Francis Beaufort's original wind scale was calibrated to the effects of wind on what kind of vessel?
items.explain: Beaufort based his scale on how wind affected a full-rigged warship. Later revisions added sea and land effects and other ship types.

items.question: Beaufort first devised his wind-force scale while in command of which Royal Navy ship?
items.explain: The Met Office records that Beaufort created the scale around 1806 while commanding HMS Woolwich. HMS Blossom came later, when he produced the 1810 version.

items.question: In which year did the Beaufort scale become mandatory for log entries on all Royal Navy ships?
items.explain: The Royal Navy made the scale compulsory in ship logs in 1838. The International Meteorological Committee adopted it for international use in 1874.

items.question: Which mineral is the reference mineral for hardness 5 on the Mohs scale?
items.explain: On the Mohs scale, calcite is 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5 and orthoclase 6.

items.question: Which ancient author compared the hardness of diamond and quartz in his Naturalis Historia, an early precursor of Mohs's ranking?
items.explain: Pliny the Elder compared diamond and quartz in the first century AD. Mohs later continued this ordinal ranking approach.

source.title: Friedrich Mohs and the mineral scale of hardness

items.question: Moving from corundum (9) to diamond (10) on the Mohs scale increases hardness by roughly how much?
items.explain: The Mohs scale is not linear. The step from 3 to 4 is about 25 percent, while the step from 9 to 10 is over 300 percent.

items.question: At which college library was Melvil Dewey working in 1873 when he began developing his classification system?
items.explain: Dewey began developing the system at the Amherst College Library in 1873. He published the first edition in 1876.

source.title: Of Note: Registering the Dewey Decimal System at the Library of Congress

items.question: In 1930, which institution began printing Dewey Decimal numbers on its catalog cards?
items.explain: OCLC's timeline records that the Library of Congress began printing Dewey numbers on catalog cards in 1930.

items.question: In what form did the first edition of the Dewey Decimal Classification appear in 1876?
answers: Under Dewey's name as a 300-page book
As a set of printed catalogue cards
As an official report for Congress
items.explain: The first edition was issued anonymously as a short pamphlet. Dewey's name only appeared on the second edition in 1885.

items.question: What was the Rubik's Cube originally called when it was first sold in Hungary?
items.explain: Ernő Rubik's puzzle was first sold in Hungary as the Magic Cube (Bűvös kocka). It was renamed Rubik's Cube for the 1980 international launch.

items.question: How long did it take Ernő Rubik to solve his own scrambled cube for the first time?
items.explain: Britannica says it took Rubik a month to solve the prototype cube after scrambling it.

items.question: Ernő Rubik's father, also named Ernő, was best known for designing which type of craft?
items.explain: The Smithsonian says Rubik's father was an aircraft engineer known for his glider designs.

source.title: A Twist of Fate: The Invention of the Rubik's Cube

items.question: In which year did Ernő Rubik apply for a Hungarian patent for his Magic Cube?
items.explain: Rubik applied for the Hungarian patent on 30 January 1975, the year after he invented the cube.

items.question: Which toy company signed the 1979 deal to release the Magic Cube worldwide?
items.explain: Rubik's partners signed with Ideal Toys in September 1979. Ideal then rebranded the puzzle as Rubik's Cube.

items.question: Louis Braille adapted a dot-based code originally devised for military use by which man?
items.explain: Braille learned of Charles Barbier's tangible dot-writing system at his school. He simplified it into the six-dot cell.

items.question: In what year did British and American agencies for the blind agree on Standard English Braille in London?
items.explain: A universal braille code for the English-speaking world was not adopted until 1932, when the agencies met in London.

items.question: In which French village was Louis Braille born?
items.explain: Louis Braille was born on 4 January 1809 in Coupvray, France.

source.title: The Story of Louis Braille: Inventor of the Braille Code

items.question: In which city was the 1884 International Meridian Conference, which recommended Greenwich as the prime meridian, held?
items.explain: The conference met in Washington, D.C., in October 1884. A geodetic conference in Rome the year before had settled most technical details.

items.question: Which US president issued the invitations to the 1884 International Meridian Conference?
items.explain: Chester Arthur, the 21st president, sent out the invitations to the conference after an 1882 act of Congress authorised it.

source.title: The adoption of a Prime Meridian and the International Meridian Conference of 1884

items.question: How many nations were represented at the 1884 International Meridian Conference?
items.explain: The conference was attended by 41 delegates from 25 nations.

source.title: The adoption of a Prime Meridian and the International Meridian Conference of 1884

items.question: In which year did Pierre de Coubertin first publicly present the five-ring Olympic emblem in the Revue Olympique?
items.explain: Coubertin described the emblem and flag in the August 1913 Revue Olympique.

source.title: 1913 : First public presentation of the Five Rings Symbol.

items.question: According to Coubertin, why were the six colours of the Olympic flag, including the white background, chosen?
answers: Each colour stood for one continent
They echoed banners of the ancient Greek Games
They were the colours of the first medals awarded
Every national flag could be reproduced with them
items.correct: Every national flag could be reproduced with them
items.explain: Coubertin said the combined colours reproduce those of every nation's flag. The individual rings do not stand for particular continents.

source.title: What Do the Olympic Rings Symbolize?

items.question: An early Sholes typewriter layout read 'QWE.TY'. What character stood where the R is today?
items.explain: The 1872 Sholes machine had a period where R now sits. The layout was later altered into QWERTY.

source.title: Where Did the QWERTY Keyboard Layout Come From?

items.question: In 1873, Christopher Sholes sold the manufacturing rights to his typewriter to which company?
items.explain: Sholes sold the rights to Remington, which developed the machine further and popularised the QWERTY layout.

source.title: Where Did the QWERTY Keyboard Layout Come From?

items.question: In which year did Alfred Nobel obtain his Swedish patent for dynamite?
items.explain: Nobel's dynamite patent dates from 1867. In 1863 he patented nitroglycerin as an industrial explosive, and in 1887 ballistite.

source.title: The man behind the prize – Alfred Nobel

items.question: Nobel made nitroglycerin safe to handle by blending it with which absorbent material?
items.explain: Nobel found that nitroglycerin mixed into diatomaceous earth was stable and easy to use, and he called the result dynamite.

source.title: Alfred Nobel gave us armaments and achievement prizes

items.question: How many patents did Alfred Nobel hold during his lifetime?
items.explain: Nobel held 355 patents over his life.

items.question: Alfred Nobel's first patent, filed in England in 1857, was for which device?
items.explain: His first patent was an English one for a gas meter. His first Swedish patent, in 1863, covered ways to prepare gunpowder.

items.question: Which institution established the prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel in 1968?
items.explain: Sweden's central bank, Sveriges Riksbank, established the economics prize in 1968. It was not one of the original prizes in Nobel's will.

items.question: In which city was Alfred Nobel & Co., the company that became Dynamit Nobel, founded in 1865?
items.explain: Nobel founded Alfred Nobel & Co. in Hamburg on 21 June 1865. Dynamit Nobel AG grew out of it.

items.question: Nobel's blasting cap was a copper capsule filled with which compound?
items.explain: Nobel's blasting cap was a copper capsule filled with mercury fulminate and set off by a fuse wire.

items.question: In which year was Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, the forerunner of Monopoly, patented?
items.explain: Magie patented The Landlord's Game in 1904, three decades before Parker Brothers sold Monopoly.

items.question: How much did Parker Brothers pay in 1935 for Elizabeth Magie's Landlord's Game patent?
items.explain: Parker Brothers bought her patent for $500, on condition that it keep publishing The Landlord's Game.

source.title: The True History of the Monopoly Game

items.question: Which policy did Magie use The Landlord's Game to promote?
answers: A ban on private rental housing
A single tax on property owners
items.correct: A single tax on property owners
items.explain: Magie used the game to illustrate how greedy landlords could exploit tenants. She promoted the single tax as a remedy.

items.question: Who was the King's baker whose bakery on Pudding Lane was where the Great Fire of London began?
items.explain: The fire began in the early hours of 2 September 1666 in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane.

items.question: Which scientist co-designed the Monument to the Great Fire of London with Sir Christopher Wren?
items.explain: The Monument was designed by Wren and Robert Hooke. It stands 202 feet high and 202 feet from where the fire started.

source.title: The Great Fire of London Walking Trail - OneCity

items.question: According to a London walking-trail account, Pudding Lane takes its name from what?
answers: A guild of medieval pudding makers
Bread puddings baked in the lane
items.explain: The lane was named for the 'puddings' (offal) that fell from carts travelling from Eastcheap meat market to the Thames.

source.title: The Great Fire of London Walking Trail - OneCity

items.question: Roughly how many people are estimated to have died in the Great Fire of London?
items.explain: Despite the huge destruction, it is estimated that only about six people died, though thousands were left homeless.

items.question: Which Frenchman falsely confessed to starting the Great Fire of London and was executed, despite not being in the city when it began?
items.explain: Robert Hubert confessed to starting the fire, but he was not in London when it began. He was executed anyway.

source.title: The Great Fire of London Walking Trail - OneCity

items.question: Which French army engineer officer discovered the Rosetta Stone in 1799?
items.explain: Bouchard, an engineer officer in Napoleon's army, took the stone from an old wall being demolished at Fort Julien near Rashid (Rosetta).

items.question: The decree inscribed on the Rosetta Stone dates from the reign of which ruler?
items.explain: The stone carries a priestly decree from the reign of Ptolemy V, dated to 196 BCE.

items.question: Alongside Greek, which two scripts are carved on the Rosetta Stone?
items.explain: The stone carries the same text in Egyptian hieroglyphic, Egyptian demotic and Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, which made the other two scripts decipherable.

source.title: 15. The Rosetta Stone - The Linda Hall

items.question: What did Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit use to set the zero point of his temperature scale?
answers: The freezing point of pure water
The temperature of a deep winter cellar
The coldest temperature of an ice-and-salt mixture
The boiling point of strong spirits
items.correct: The coldest temperature of an ice-and-salt mixture
items.explain: Fahrenheit set zero at the lowest temperature he could produce by mixing ice and common salt.

items.question: On the Fahrenheit scale, into how many equal parts is the interval between water's freezing and boiling points divided?
items.explain: Water freezes at 32°F and boils at 212°F, and the 180 degrees between them are equal parts.

items.question: In which year was the name 'centigrade' replaced by 'Celsius' for the temperature scale?
items.explain: The scale was known as centigrade until 1948, when the Celsius name was adopted as the international standard.

items.question: At which event did Whitcomb Judson exhibit his 'clasp locker', an early zipper, in 1893?
answers: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago
items.correct: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago
items.explain: Judson showed his hook-and-eye slide fastener at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

items.question: Which company's employee coined the word 'zipper' in 1923 for its overshoes?
items.explain: The term was coined in 1923 by B.G. Work of the B.F. Goodrich Company for use on overshoes.

items.question: In which year was Gideon Sundback's patent for the forerunner of the modern brass-toothed zipper granted?
items.explain: Sundback developed his metal-toothed fastener in 1913, and his patent followed in 1917.

items.question: In British and French heraldry, what are arms that break the rule of tincture called?
items.explain: Arms that put metal on metal or colour on colour are called armes fausses (or armes à enquérir).
